This microscope is insane.

Look at the difference between these two images! Both are of a cell’s nucleus, but this one was taken with a SUPER-RESOLUTION microscope.

Regular microscopes can only see down to about 250 nanometers, past that, the wavelengths of visible light are bigger than what we’re trying to see so light waves diffract and spread out

Every year about 2.7 million people are bitten by venomous snakes. When this venom enters your bloodstream, in minutes or hours, it can cause tissue and neurological damage.

The only way to counteract this is with antivenom, which attaches to the components of venom and blocks it from binding to tissues, blood cells, or nerves.

Why do all the planes fly this line?

If the shortest path across the Atlantic is here, why do all the planes fly on a different path?

At the equator, the ground is moving about 1,600 kilometers per hour, but at the poles, it’s zero. So when the warm air flows from the equator to the poles, it starts to outrun the ground below it and curve!

This is the “jet stream” and thanks to modern tech, we can fit so many planes in this relatively tiny wind column to give them a boost!

My next Ukiyo-e interpreted in #sashiko ! The original is Japanese woodblock is titled “RETURNING HOME” dating back to 1915. It was made by Fritz Capelari. The depiction shows a large group of colorfully dressed women walking home in the rain. All of them are carrying large traditional umbrellas, which are partly blocking our view. These beautifully ornamented umbrellas are of course the image’s main motive, but linking them to a Tokyo street scene is what truly brings out their elegance and diversity. The colors are amazingly fresh and reveal the intensity of Fritz Capelari’s art! Swipe to see my humble interpretation of this done by hand in #sashiko style. Do you like it?

I have always loved #Ukiyo-e a genre of Japanese woodblock prints and paintings from the 17th-19th centuries. “The Great Wave off Kanagawa” is a woodblock print by the Japanese ukiyo-e Master Hokusai, created in late 1831 during the Edo period of Japanese history. The print depicts three boats moving through a storm-tossed sea, with a large, cresting wave forming a spiral in the centre over the boats and Mount Fuji in the background. Only about 100 prints, in varying conditions, are thought to have survived into the 21st century.
The Great Wave off Kanagawa has been described as “possibly the most reproduced image in the history of all art”as well as being a contender for the “most famous artwork in Japanese history. I saw a print of this art work at the Chicago Art Institute  with my friend @iluvpepero I was mesmerized by its simplicity, detail and how it conveys the power and strength of the ocean and nature.

I was stuck at home quite sick the past few weeks and decided to create something new… you know make lemonade when life gives you lemons etc 😉 I used #Sashiko techniques to create a coaster with The Great Wave. It was so hard to get the colors and scale on a small 4X4 inch fabric. But I am happy the way it turned out. What do you guys think?

One of the best career moves for men is to have children (the make on average 6% more per child) while for women it’s the worst career move (they make 4% less per child). 

Shelley J. Correll, a sociology professor at Stanford University found that employers were less likely to call back a woman if she was a mother and offered $11,000 less than childless women and $13,000 less than fathers. 

On the other hand, men *with kids were more likely to get a call back than men *without* kids. That’s why there’s a motherhood penalty but a fatherhood bonus, and that this mom tax is five times higher for for low-income women. 

One thing men can do to remedy this is to take on more parenting and talk about it in the workplace. When a mother leaves early she’s assumed to leave for childcare while when a man leaves early he’s assumed to leave for a work-related event. Men need to be open and honest about the role they’re taking in the home. 

The most effective way to minimize these draconian inequalities is paid parental leave and universal child care, something we should all unite for ✊❤️

Every girl who has walked into a @girlswhocode classroom owes something to Margaret Hamilton.

In the 1960s, before “software engineering” was even a term (she’s the one who coined it), Margaret led the MIT team that wrote the code that landed Apollo 11 on the moon. And she did it as a working mom. She brought her young daughter to the lab on nights and weekends.

That’s the story I tell girls who wonder if they belong in tech. Margaret shot for the stars and got us to the moon. Rest in peace 🤍

The national conversation has focused on consent education. Are we teaching it early enough? Are we teaching it right? But what keeps me up at night are the more than 50 young men in that group chat, and the bravery deficit in their silence.

I want to raise sons who speak up instead of closing their screens.

America made motherhood look impossible. But it’s not impossible everywhere.

Other countries recognize that caring for children takes time, money, and support.

Meanwhile, the U.S. is the only industrialized nation without national paid leave, and too many parents are going into debt just to make childcare work.

#NoCountryforMothers is about asking why motherhood in America is so different and what it will take to build a country that actually supports families.

Host a watch party or find one near you at the link in bio.

The message to moms is clear: the responsibility is yours. The power is not.

We are expected to raise the next generation, but the people making decisions about our schools, our economy, our safety, and our families? Too often, they are not us.

#NoCountryforMothers is about naming the impossible choices mothers have been handed and refusing to accept it.

How did we clever humans build all of that? We went from hunter-gatherers to a civilization that can space travel and has a chance to colonize other planets and reach out toward the stars 🤯

View of Earth from 900 million miles away, with Saturn's rings in the image, taken by Cassini spacecraft.

That dot is us, all 8 billion of us. It's all an insanely lucky miracle.

I'm grateful for all of it & all of you. Love you all! ❤️

Over the past several weeks, I've been back in the lab working crazy hours like old times, and loving life. This was much needed. I'm happy ;-)

I need both literature & engineering in my life 🤣 I love both, and both are a source of truth.

I'm still doing the podcast, just adding much more engineering back into the mix ;-) The podcast gives me an opportunity to celebrate great scientists, engineers, and builders. This is one of the things I love doing most.

In the coming months, I'll continue splitting time between MIT and Caltech (Boston & LA) working with some brilliant people. The focus of the work is human-robot interaction with quadrupeds and humanoid robots.

I think humans are beautiful and fascinating and for the most part awesome.

The internet seems to want to tell you otherwise. I disagree, but I don't have the right words for it.

I'll probably do a long solo episode on Dostoevsky (especially Brothers Karamazov) at some point to help me articulate this better.

We humans are a good bunch.
